1:
The chapter opens by unrolling a long register of the priests and Levites who came up from Babylon, and the witnesses read the bare catalogue of names as anything but bare. The reformed John Gill fixes the two leaders at its head — Zerubbabel the prince and Jeshua the high priest, the same Joshua who serves under the prophets — and notes that the names of the priests are given in this verse and the six that follow. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the architecture: this verse is the title of the first list, running through v.9, and the two-and-twenty heads here enumerated reappear, with slight variations attributable to clerical errors, as the names of the priestly houses in vv.12-21, given there with the priests who represented them in the days of Joiakim. Fifteen of these, they add, had already sealed the covenant as heads of their houses in Nehemiah 10.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry asks why so long a roll of little more than names should be inserted at all, and answers with a theology of memory: perhaps to keep in remembrance those good men, that posterity might know to whom, under God, they were beholden for the happy revival of their religion. "The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance," he urges from Psalm 112:6; and it is a debt we still owe faithful ministers to remember our guides who have spoken to us the word of God, as Hebrews 13:7 enjoins. It is good, he adds, to know what our godly ancestors were, that we may learn thereby what we should be.

The wesleyan-arminian voices attend to the courses. John Wesley identifies these as the chief of the priests, the heads of the twenty-four courses David appointed by divine direction in 1 Chronicles 24; and where there were twenty-four, here are but twenty-two, and in v.12 only twenty, because two courses had become extinct in Babylon. Adam Clarke agrees these are "not the whole, but the chief," and notes the Septuagint's many omissions.

A genuine question divides them over the third name, Ezra. Clarke holds him generally allowed to be the Ezra whose book we have read, who, if the same, must by now have been upward of a hundred years old — not improbable, since an especial providence might preserve so useful a man. Henry supposes rather that this is neither Jeremiah the prophet nor Ezra the scribe, whose fame lay long before and some time after. The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, takes the middle ground: Seraiah is the family name represented by Jeshua, and of Jeremiah and Ezra "we know nothing more than this record gives."
2:
The list of priests runs on with a second file of names — Amariah, Malluch, Hattush — and the witnesses read them through the grid of the ancient priestly courses. The reformed John Gill notes that these names are found among the sealers of the covenant in Nehemiah 10, and marks a small variation to be watched through the whole register: the Malluch here is the Melicu who reappears at v.14, the same house under a slightly altered form. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set these heads within the larger pattern, for the two-and-twenty names gathered in these opening verses are the same that recur, house by house, as the priestly families of vv.12-21, matched there with the men who headed them in the days of Joiakim.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley supplies the framework that makes sense of the count. These are the heads of the courses David established by divine direction in 1 Chronicles 24; and whereas David appointed twenty-four, here are but twenty-two, and in v.12 only twenty, because two of the courses had died out in the captivity, and two of the persons named in these verses — Hattush among them — left no posterity to carry their house forward into the next generation. Adam Clarke adds that this roll gives "not the whole, but the chief" of the priests, and that the Septuagint omits several of the names outright, a reminder of how the catalogue has suffered in the copying.

The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, reads such names as family names rather than the tale of individuals — the house standing under the name of its founder — and it is on that footing that a single name can pass down two and three generations, borne now by the head who sealed the covenant, now by his son who represents the house in Joiakim's day. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry would not have the reader hurry past even these unexplained names, for the whole register was set down, he judges, to keep the memory of faithful ministers alive, that posterity might know to whom, under God, they owed the reviving of their religion.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the sealers and the Malluch-Melicu variation, Keil the correspondence with the later list, Wesley and Clarke the courses and their attrition, Ellicott the family names, Henry the memorial purpose; together they turn three otherwise silent names into a window on the ordered priesthood that David had numbered, and that the return was carefully restoring, course by course, so far as the captivity had left it whole.
6:
The catalogue of priestly heads reaches a small hinge at "Shemaiah, and Joiarib, Jedaiah," and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott alone pauses over a single connecting word. The "and" that stands before Joiarib, he observes, begins the list of those who did not seal the covenant — a like "and" marking the same division at v.19. The register, in other words, is not a random file but is quietly ordered: the heads who had subscribed the great agreement of Nehemiah 10 are set down first, and this conjunction turns the reader to those who, for whatever reason, had not put their seal to it.

That ordering rests on the observation the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch had made at the head of the list: of the two-and-twenty heads here enumerated, fifteen had already sealed the covenant as heads of their houses, so that the names divide between the sealers and the rest. The little "and" before Joiarib is the seam between the two groups, and the fact that the historian preserved so fine a distinction is itself a token of the care with which the roll was kept.

The reformed John Gill reads the same names as belonging among the sealers and the chief of the priests whose courses the return was labouring to restore, of most of whom nothing now survives but the name and the office. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps before the reader the frame that governs the whole file — that these are the heads of the twenty-four courses David appointed in 1 Chronicles 24, thinned now to twenty-two by the losses of the captivity — so that even a name like Joiarib or Jedaiah stands for a whole ministering house, its turn in the temple service reaching back to David's ordinance.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the obscure entry its worth. The register was written, he holds, to keep the memory of faithful ministers alive, that posterity might know to whom, under God, they owed the revival of their religion; and it is a debt we still owe our guides who have spoken to us the word of God, as Hebrews 13:7 enjoins. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott fixes the dividing "and," Keil the sealers behind it, Gill and Wesley the courses these names head, Henry the abiding purpose of the record; and between them they make of a bare line a proof that God kept account even of which of his priests had, and had not, sealed the covenant — and forgot the name of none.
7:
The first roll of priestly heads closes with "Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, Jedaiah," and the subscription "These were the chief of the priests in the days of Jeshua," and the witnesses gather around the courses these names represent. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the frame: the chief of the priests were the four-and-twenty orders or courses, all subordinate to each other as David had established them in 1 Chronicles 24, and these orders continued in force, he notes, right down to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans. The list here is the head of that long institution, its founders come home from exile to take up again the ancient rotation of the temple.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott enters a careful qualification. "These were the chief," he grants, but genealogically, not according to the courses — for the courses, he observes, are complete in none of the lists that have come down to us. The register names heads of houses by descent; it does not lay out the twenty-four divisions in their full order, several of which the captivity had left broken. The other grammatical-historical witness, Keil and Delitzsch, reads the same subscription as the seal upon the first list, "the heads of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua" — the brethren being the Levites, their fellow-tribesmen and assistants — and it is these very heads, they remind us, that reappear as the priestly houses of vv.12-21 in the next generation.

The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keep the arithmetic in view. Where David had numbered twenty-four courses, the return could muster but twenty-two, two having become extinct in Babylon; and of these twenty-two, only twenty would leave sons to head their houses in Joiakim's day, Hattush and one other passing without posterity. So even the completed list carries within it the marks of loss — a priesthood restored, but not wholly, a rotation resumed with gaps that could not be filled.

The witnesses do not finally divide, though Clarke presses the continuity of David's courses and Ellicott their incompleteness. Both are true at once: the institution endured, and yet no surviving roll preserves it whole. What they share is the sense that this quiet subscription marks a real achievement — the chief priestly houses gathered again under their ancient heads in the days of Jeshua, the temple's ordered service set once more upon the foundation David had laid, so far as a returning and diminished people could restore it.
8:
The register turns from the priests to the Levites of the same generation — "Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, which was over the thanksgiving" — and the witnesses fasten chiefly on the last office named. The reformed John Gill notes simply that these Levites lived in the same times as the priests just listed. The wesleyan-arminian voices explain the charge laid on Mattaniah: Adam Clarke glosses "over the thanksgiving" as chief of the principal singers, referring the reader to the like office at Nehemiah 11:17; and John Wesley reads it as a standing trust — Mattaniah was to see that the psalms of thanksgiving were continually sung in the temple, in due time and manner, so that the house of God should never lack its appointed praise.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fill in the identities and the small textual difficulties. Of these Levitical heads, Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, and Sherebiah appear among those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 10, and Sherebiah with Jeshua the son of Kadmiel recur as heads of Levites at v.24. The name "Judah," which occurs in none of the other Levitical lists, they take to be miswritten for Hodiah. Mattaniah they identify with the Asaphite of Nehemiah 11:17, the son of Micah, head of the first band of singers — for he was, in the phrase of the text, over the singing of praise.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they mark how much of the Levites' whole vocation is caught up in that one office. The thanksgiving was not an occasional thing but a continual ministry, entrusted to a named man and his brethren, kept in due course and order so that the temple's song should be unbroken. The same Mattaniah who sealed his people's covenant with God stands here over the praise of God; the same heads who bound themselves to the law are set to lead the house in thanks.

It is a fitting note on which the register of the returning ministers should dwell, for the chapter will end in a great outburst of exactly this thanksgiving, when two companies of singers walk the dedicated wall. The men numbered here in a dry catalogue are the very order whose office it was to make Israel's gratitude vocal; and the witnesses, in tracing Mattaniah from the sealed covenant to the choir, quietly bind the roll of names to the joy that is coming, the guardians of the thanksgiving named long before the thanksgiving is heard.
9:
Two more Levites are added — "Bakbukiah and Unni, their brethren, were over against them in the watches" — and the witnesses read in that phrase the pattern of antiphonal praise. The reformed John Gill notes only that these were two further Levites, the first of them named again in the muster of Nehemiah 11:17. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw out what "over against them" implies: Bakbukiah and Unni, their brethren, stood opposite the company of Mattaniah, forming in the service the answering choir. The word rendered "watches," they insist, is not to be understood of watch-posts, for v.24 forbids it; it denotes rather the divisions of service, the two bands of singers set face to face to take up the praise by turns.

Keil and Delitzsch mark two further details. The absence of the doorkeepers from this Levitical list is, they say, remarkable, when one compares the fuller reckoning elsewhere; and while Bakbukiah will recur among the Levites of a later day at v.24, the name Unni is met with nowhere else, though there is no ground, on that account, for emending it away. The register preserves the man though it tells us nothing more of him.

The witnesses do not divide, and the picture they leave is of a worship built on responsion. The singers did not chant in a single undifferentiated mass but in two companies, ward answering ward, one choir lifting the psalm and the other answering it — the very arrangement David had laid down, and the very shape the dedication of the wall will take when two great thanksgiving processions move in opposite directions round the city and meet at last in the house of God.

So the quiet notice of Bakbukiah and Unni "over against" their brethren is more than a filling-out of the roll. It fixes, in the days of Jeshua, the same antiphonal order that the chapter's climax will display on a grand scale; the two Levites standing opposite the two make in miniature what the two companies on the wall will make in full. The witnesses, tracing the phrase to its right sense, keep the reader from mistaking a musical arrangement for a mere watch of the gates, and let the little verse foreshadow the answering songs of praise in which the whole solemnity will culminate. And it is worth marking that the register troubles to name even Unni, of whom nothing else is known — a man preserved in Scripture for no deed of his own but his place in the answering choir, that the order of praise might be handed down entire.
10:
The register pauses to trace the high-priestly line — "Jeshua begat Joiakim, Joiakim Eliashib, Eliashib Joiada, Joiada Jonathan, and Jonathan Jaddua" — and the witnesses read the genealogy as a kind of chronological spine. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains why it was inserted: a catalogue of the Jewish high priests was now the more necessary, since the times of the second temple were to be measured no longer by the years of kings, as formerly, but by the succession of high priests. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make the same point structurally: the line from Jeshua to Jaddua is set here as a connecting link between the lists of Levites, to explain the dates that define them — the roll of v.1 belonging to the time of Jeshua, and that of vv.12-21 to the days of Joiakim and his successors.

Keil and Delitzsch add a sharp historical gloss. The "Jonathan" of this verse, they show from vv.22-23, is a clerical error for Johanan — the Greek Johannes — of whom Josephus tells the dark tale that he murdered his own brother Jesus within the temple, and so gave the Persian general Bagoses a pretext for grievous measures against the Jews. The sacred line was not untouched by the crimes of its holders.

The reformed John Gill presses the question of authorship. If the last-named Jaddua is the Jaddus who, in Josephus, went out in his pontifical robes to meet Alexander the Great after the conquest of Tyre and Gaza, then this paragraph can hardly have been written by Nehemiah, who could scarcely have lived so long. Gill judges it a fragment inserted by some godly man under divine direction in later times, as the books of Moses and Joshua carry similar insertions — the succession being carried on past Nehemiah's own day by a later inspired hand.

The witnesses do not finally divide over the substance, though Gill's insertion-argument goes further than Keil's quieter talk of a connecting note. What they agree on is the purpose the genealogy serves: it fixes the several lists in time, hanging each roll of ministers upon the high priest under whom it was drawn, from Jeshua of the restoration to Jaddua of Alexander's day. The line of priests becomes the calendar of the restored nation, and the historian, by threading it through the register, gives the reader the measure by which all these otherwise timeless names of priests and Levites are to be dated and understood.
11:
The high-priestly line is carried to its end — "Joiada begat Jonathan, and Jonathan begat Jaddua" — and the witnesses attend to a corrupted name and to the famous figure who closes the succession. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the text at once: the "Jonathan" here should be Johanan, as v.22 makes plain, and the Jaddua who follows is most probably the high priest who confronted Alexander the Great. The other grammatical-historical witness, Keil and Delitzsch, treats the whole passage as a connecting note explaining the dates of the Levitical lists, the succession from Jeshua reaching down to Jaddua precisely so that the several rolls of vv.12-21 and vv.22-26 may each be fixed to their proper high priest.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the encounter that has made Jaddua's name memorable. He is, Clarke holds, the high priest who went out with his brethren in pontifical robes to meet Alexander as he advanced upon Jerusalem after the fall of Tyre and Gaza with the purpose of destroying it; so struck was the conqueror by the priest's appearance that he forbore all hostility, prostrated himself before Jaddua, worshipped the Lord at the temple, and granted the Jews many privileges — a scene Clarke draws from Josephus and from Prideaux. The last name in a dry genealogy thus opens upon one of the great providential deliverances of the nation.

The reformed John Gill had already drawn from this reach to Alexander's day his conclusion about the passage's origin — that it must be the insertion of a later inspired hand, since Nehemiah himself could hardly have lived to see Jaddua's meeting with the Macedonian. The genealogy outruns its author, and that very fact tells us something of how the sacred books grew.

The witnesses do not divide over the reading, and their small labours converge on a single effect. A verse that seems only to add two more names to a list in fact carries the succession of the second temple down to the threshold of a new age, when the empire of Persia would give way to that of Greece, and the high priest of Jerusalem would stand, robed, before the world's conqueror. Ellicott mends the name, Keil fixes the chronology, Clarke recovers the history, Gill weighs the authorship; and together they let the reader see that the line of priests, patiently traced through these verses, ends not in obscurity but at one of the hinges of sacred history.
12:
The register turns to the next generation — "in the days of Joiakim were priests, the chief of the fathers" — and the witnesses read the second list as the sign of a ministry renewed. The reformed John Gill identifies Joiakim as the son and successor of Jeshua, the first high priest of the second temple, and runs through the twenty heads of houses named in his day, from Meraiah to Nethaneel; there are but twenty here, he notes, against the twenty-two of the fathers' generation, because two of the earlier houses — Hattush and Miamin — left no descendants to represent them. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the parallel plainly: as their fathers had been priests in the days of Joshua, so in the days of Joiakim his son the sons of those men executed the priesthood in their fathers' room, some of the fathers being yet alive and many now dead.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set this list beside the first, observing that the names of the houses in vv.12-21 answer, with slight variations, to the heads enumerated in vv.1-7 — the same families, one generation on, headed now by the sons who had stepped into their fathers' places. The register is thus a double photograph of the priesthood, taken at an interval of a lifetime, and the two frames agree.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the correspondence into praise. We have reason, he says, to acknowledge God's favour to his church and care of it in this, that as one generation of ministers passes away another comes; the men eminent in their day are here named again in their sons, so that the work of God should never fail for want of instruments. And he marks the rare mercy of it — that twenty good fathers should leave behind them twenty good sons to fill up their places, hardly to be matched in any other age.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill counts the houses and accounts for the two that failed, Wesley fixes the succession of son to father, Keil the correspondence of the two lists, Henry the goodness of the God who provides. Together they make of a repeated catalogue a quiet doctrine of providence: the temple's service handed on unbroken from Jeshua's priests to Joiakim's, the same houses ministering under the same names, a whole generation of faithful men succeeded by another as faithful — and the God of the covenant seen in the very continuity of the roll.
13:
The list of Joiakim's priests proceeds head by head — "of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Jehohanan" — and the witnesses read the matched pairs of father-house and son-head as the register's careful bookkeeping of the priesthood. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, who lay the two lists side by side, treat these verses as the roll of the priestly houses and their heads already explained in conjunction with vv.1-7 — each ancient house named first, and against it the man who headed it in Joiakim's day. The correspondence is exact enough to be checked house by house, and where it wavers the cause is the ordinary slip of a hand-copied text.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses that last point, for the names do not always answer cleanly between the generations; he will note at v.14 that the Melicu here is the Malluch of v.2, and elsewhere that "some name has dropped out," anomalies of which, he candidly owns, no account can now be given. The register is faithful, but it is old, and it bears the marks of long transmission.

The reformed John Gill keeps the tally in view — twenty heads in Joiakim's day where the fathers' generation had twenty-two, the houses of Hattush and Miamin having failed of descendants — and reminds the reader that of most of these men nothing survives but the name and the office they held.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry redeems the dryness with a note of wonder he had struck over the whole list: it is a rare instance, he says, that twenty good fathers should leave behind them twenty good sons to fill up their places, and it is God's own favour to his church that as one generation of ministers passes away another comes. The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott weigh the correspondence and its blemishes, Gill counts the houses, Henry blesses the God who continues them; and between them they make of a column of paired names a lesson at once in textual patience and in providence — a priesthood handed down son to father, its record kept so exactly that even a dropped or altered name is marked, and its continuance owned as the gift of the God who never leaves his house without a servant. So even a column of matched names, dry to the careless eye, becomes in their hands a double witness: to the patience with which the sacred text was copied and kept, and to the faithfulness with which one generation of ministers was raised up to follow another.
14:
The roll of Joiakim's priests runs on — "of Melicu, Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph" — and here the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott pauses to reconcile a name and to confess a puzzle. The Melicu of this verse, he observes, is the "Malluch" of v.2, the same house under an altered spelling; and Hattush, who stood in that earlier list, is here omitted altogether. Other anomalies of this kind may be noticed through the register, he adds, of which no account can now be given — the honest verdict of a critic who will neither hide the difficulty nor manufacture a solution.

The omission of Hattush is not, however, without its reason, and the reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley supply it. Where the fathers' generation numbered twenty-two heads, Joiakim's numbers but twenty, because two of the houses — Hattush among them — left no posterity to represent them; so the name that appeared in the first list rightly drops from the second, the house having died out. What Ellicott records as an anomaly is, in this instance, the register faithfully recording a real extinction.

The other grammatical-historical witness, Keil and Delitzsch, gathers the smaller divergences of spelling under a single head: the names of the houses in vv.12-21 answer to the heads of vv.1-7 with slight variations attributable to clerical errors, the ordinary marks of a document long copied by hand. Melicu for Malluch is just such a variation; the substance of the house is untouched though the letters shift.

The witnesses do not divide, and their patience with the imperfect text is itself instructive. A less careful record might have smoothed the names into agreement or quietly filled the gap where Hattush had stood; this one lets the variant spelling and the missing house both stand, and the commentators, rather than emend, set the readings side by side and own what they cannot explain. Ellicott fixes the identity of Melicu and marks the anomaly, Gill and Wesley account for the vanished Hattush, Keil files the whole under the slips of transmission; and between them they make of two paired names a small lesson in the fidelity of Scripture, which preserves even the flaws and the losses of the priestly line rather than tidy them away. The register might have smoothed Melicu back into Malluch and quietly restored the vanished Hattush; that it did neither is, to the witnesses, a mark of its honesty, and they follow its example, recording the variant and the loss rather than mending them.
17:
The list of priestly heads reaches "of Abijah, Zichri; of Miniamin, of Moadiah, Piltai," and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes at once what is wrong with it: against Miniamin no name of a head is given, so that, in his plain words, "some name has dropped out." The register, faithful as it is, has here suffered a real loss in transmission — a house named, but the man who headed it fallen out of the text, leaving a gap that no copy now recovers.

The other grammatical-historical witness, Keil and Delitzsch, sets such a blemish within the general character of the roll. The names of Joiakim's priestly houses in vv.12-21 answer to the heads of vv.1-7 with variations attributable to clerical errors; the omission of a head against Miniamin is one more such slip, the ordinary mark of a document long copied by hand. The witnesses do not hide it, nor do they emend it away; they let the defective line stand and name the defect for what it is.

The reformed John Gill keeps the frame that steadies the reader through these obscure entries — that the register sets down the returning priests house by house, by the ancestor from whom they sprang, and that of most of them nothing now remains but the bare designation. Where even the designation is broken, as here, the loss is owned rather than concealed.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the dry and even damaged line above the counting-house. The whole register, he holds, was written to keep the memory of faithful ministers alive, that posterity might know to whom, under God, they were beholden for the reviving of their religion; and it is good to know what our godly predecessors were, that we may learn what we should be. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott marks the dropped name, Keil files it among the slips of a hand-copied text, Gill keeps the register's character, Henry its abiding purpose; and between them they make of a broken entry a curious proof of Scripture's honesty. The sacred record might have quietly supplied the missing head; instead it hands down the very gap, and the commentators hand it down after, unwilling to gild a text that God saw fit to preserve, blemish and all, for the honour of the priestly houses it names. A house named without its head is still a house remembered; and the God who kept so careful a roll of his ministers did not disdain to hand down even its imperfections, that nothing true might be lost.
22:
The register turns to the Levites of a later day — "the Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, and Johanan, and Jaddua, were recorded chief of the fathers: also the priests, to the reign of Darius the Persian" — and the witnesses divide the labour between chronology and identity. The reformed John Gill fixes the frame: Eliashib was the third high priest of the second temple, and it is in his days and those of his successors that this list of Levitical heads was drawn. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as at once the title of the following list of Levites and, in its latter clause, the subscription of the preceding list of priests, the heads being recorded down "under the reign of Darius the Persian" — a phrase that fixes the outer limit of the record.

The naming of Jaddua carries the reader again to Alexander's day, and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke rehearses the great scene: Jaddua is probably the high priest who met the conqueror in his pontifical robes after the fall of Tyre and Gaza, so that Alexander forbore to harm Jerusalem, worshipped at the temple, and granted the Jews many privileges, as Josephus and Prideaux relate.

But which Darius is meant? Here the witnesses openly differ. Clarke reports the two rival identifications without deciding between them: Calmet maintained it must be Darius Codomanus, the last Persian king, whom Alexander defeated; but Archbishop Usher understood it of the earlier Darius Nothus, in whose reign he thought Jaddua was born. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes Usher's side outright — the Darius here is Nothus, and this Jaddua may therefore be the father of the Jaddua who lived in the days of Darius Codomanus and of Alexander the Great, so that the difficulty of dating the passage is eased.

The debate is real and turns on the whole date of the list: if Codomanus, the record reaches to the very eve of the Greek conquest and cannot be Nehemiah's own; if Nothus, it may stand nearer his time, with the famous Jaddua a generation later still. The witnesses do not resolve it, but the resolution matters, for it bears on how far beyond Nehemiah's lifetime the register runs. Gill and Keil fix the Levites and the subscription, Clarke sets the two Dariuses side by side, Wesley chooses Nothus and eases the chronology; and between them they leave the reader with a list of ministers reaching, by one reckoning or another, to the very border of the Persian age.
23:
The record of the Levites is anchored to an older document — "the sons of Levi, the chief of the fathers, were written in the book of the chronicles, even until the days of Johanan the son of Eliashib" — and the witnesses ask first what that book was. The reformed John Gill reports that some refer it to the canonical Chronicles; but the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke answers flatly that this cannot be our book of Chronicles, since no such list is found there, but must be some other register or public record, now lost. The genealogy of the Levites, in other words, once stood in an official archive that has not survived, and Nehemiah draws upon it here.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sense forward into the office it introduces. The chief of the Levites — Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua the son of Kadmiel (the "son" here, they judge, a gloss to be expunged) — stood with their brethren over against them "to praise and to give thanks, according to the commandment of David the man of God," an ordinance they trace to 1 Chronicles 16:4 and 1 Chronicles 23:30. The phrase "ward over against ward," used elsewhere of the gatekeepers, is here applied to the position of the answering companies of singers — the same antiphonal arrangement met already at v.9.

So the verse does double duty: it cites a lost chronicle to authenticate the Levitical succession down to Johanan, and it sets that succession in the act of praise for which the Levites existed. The register is not merely genealogical; it is liturgical, tracing the men whose office was to keep the temple's thanksgiving in its ordered courses.

The witnesses do not sharply divide, though Gill and Clarke differ mildly over the identity of the source-book. What they agree on is the weight the verse gives to record and to precedent: the Levites' names were kept in a public register, and their service ran "according to the commandment of David," so that neither the men nor their manner of worship was left to improvisation. Gill and Clarke fix the lost chronicle, Keil the answering choirs and their Davidic warrant; and between them they show a restored ministry that looked backward for its authority — to an archive for its pedigree and to David for its praise — even as it looked forward to the great thanksgiving the chapter is about to describe.
24:
The thread of the narrative, broken by the citation of the old chronicle, is taken up again with the Levites, and the witnesses mark the resumption. "And the chief of the Levites," the verse begins, and the reformed John Gill reads it as the point where Nehemiah's history, interrupted by the two preceding notes, is carried on from the priests to the Levites in the times of the third high priest. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the same turn: the account resumes with the Levites and gives a list of the temple's serving officers, many of the names being the same as in earlier times — the ministry continuous, the men recurring.

The office itself is the heart of the verse, and the other grammatical-historical witness, Keil and Delitzsch, sets it out. The heads named — Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua, with Kadmiel (the "son" before his name they judge a gloss and would strike) — are the familiar leaders of the Levitical orders, met already among the sealers of the covenant and the singers of v.8. Set opposite them stood their brethren, whose charge it was "to praise and to give thanks, according to the commandment of David the man of God," the two companies ordered "ward over against ward," as at v.9 — the answering choirs that David had appointed and that 1 Chronicles 23:30 had prescribed to stand every morning and evening to thank and praise the Lord.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gathers up the whole burden of the register of Levites. What these men were for was praise; their divisions, their standing face to face, their very existence as an order, all served the single end of keeping the thanksgiving of the house of God in its appointed course. The names are old and recurring because the office is fixed and enduring, handed down from generation to generation under the pattern David laid.

Gill and Ellicott fix the resumption and the continuity of the men, Keil the answering companies and their Davidic warrant; and together they let the reader see the Levites not as a list to be endured but as a choir to be heard. The register, in naming the chief of the Levites and their brethren over against them, is quietly assembling the very singers who, a few verses on, will walk the dedicated wall in two great companies and fill Jerusalem with a thanksgiving heard afar off.
25:
The list closes with the doorkeepers — "Mattaniah, and Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, Akkub, were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates" — and the witnesses gather around the humble but vital office of the gate. The reformed John Gill notes simply that these kept watch at the gates of the temple; the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add that the porters kept ward "at the thresholds of the gates," and that the following verse, v.26, forms the final subscription of the two lists in vv.12-21 and vv.24-25, closing the whole register of ministers.

The one real question is what these "thresholds" were, and here the witnesses part. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confesses himself puzzled by those who make them a kind of portico, since no such porticoes are elsewhere mentioned; he proposes rather that they resembled watch-boxes, temporary and moveable shelters for the men who took care of the gates — for common sense, he says, dictates that some such convenience must have existed. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes the word quite otherwise, glossing "at the thresholds" as "at the treasuries," the store-chambers attached to the several gates of the temple, so that the porters kept ward not merely at the doors but over the stores lodged beside them.

The difference is small but genuine: were these men huddled in watch-shelters at the gates, or set as guardians over the gate-treasuries? Clarke reasons from practical necessity, Ellicott from the sense of the Hebrew term; and the text leaves room for both, the porter's charge being at once to keep the door and to guard what lay within it.

Beneath the dispute the witnesses agree on the dignity of the office. To keep the ward of the gates was to preserve the purity of the house, denying entrance to whatever was unclean — a charge the chapter will honour again at v.45, where the porters keep "the ward of the purification." Gill fixes the watch, Keil the closing subscription, Clarke and Ellicott the debated thresholds; and together they let even the doorkeepers take their place in the register, the last-named and lowliest of the temple's servants, yet set to guard the very holiness of the sanctuary they served. The office was menial in the world's eyes and glorious in the temple's, for to stand at the threshold and turn back the unclean was to keep the house of God undefiled; and the six men here named, obscure as they are, held that trust as truly as the priests held theirs.
26:
The long register is sealed with a dating subscription — "these were in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor, and of Ezra the priest, the scribe" — and the witnesses read it as the formal close of the whole catalogue. The reformed John Gill traces the pedigree it names: Joiakim was the son of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, who had been high priest in Babylon, so that the grandson of the exile now held the office in the restored temple — the priesthood carried unbroken across the captivity from Jozadak in Babylon to Joiakim in Jerusalem.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the verse's office: it is the final subscription of the two lists, the priests of vv.12-21 and the Levites of vv.24-25, dating both to the generation of Joiakim and to the days of Nehemiah and Ezra. The register is thus anchored to three named authorities at once — a high priest, a governor, and a scribe — and by them set firmly in time.

That triple naming is not idle, for it binds the whole roll of ministers to the two great reformers whose labours the book records. Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe stand together here, as they will stand together on the dedicated wall, the civil and the sacred leaders of the return; and the lists of priests and Levites are certified as the record of their day, the men they gathered and set in order for the service of the house.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, surveying these closing notices, had seen in the whole register a memorial of God's care for his church — some of these Levites singers, others porters, all according to the command of David — and a debt of remembrance owed to faithful ministers. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the descent from Jozadak, Keil the subscription's function, Henry its memorial worth; and together they let the register end as it began, not in a mere heap of names but in a dated and authenticated record. The priests and Levites of the second temple are here numbered, generation by generation, under their high priests and their reformers, and handed on to posterity as the servants through whom, under God, the worship of Israel was restored — the roll of the ministry set down, and sealed with the names of Joiakim, Nehemiah, and Ezra.
27:
With the register complete, the chapter turns to its great scene — the dedication of the wall — and the witnesses feel the change of key. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets it against the labour that went before: we have read of the building of the wall with fear and trembling, and here is the dedicating of it with joy and triumph, for "those that sow in tears shall thus reap." The dedication, he explains, was a solemn thanksgiving to God for the finished work; a devoting of the city to his honour, so that this holy city, the city of the great King of Psalm 48:2 and Matthew 5:35, was afresh given up to God; and a putting of the walls under his protection, owning that "except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain," as Psalm 127:1 declares.

The reformed John Gill and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the occasion. Gill takes the dedication to include the whole city, kept as a festival with prayer, praise, and sacrifice; the wall had been finished on the twenty-fifth of Elul, but the gates and all things were not ready till the following month, when, the Jewish writers say, the seventh of Elul was thereafter observed yearly. Keil and Delitzsch note that, the wall being finished as at Nehemiah 6:15 and the city's peopling secured, the fortification was now solemnly dedicated; the Levites were sought out of all their places to keep the dedication "with gladness," a phrase they would read, with the ancient versions, as at Ezra 6:16.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds that the solemnity was to be processional, musical, and sacrificial, after the pattern of Solomon's dedication of the temple; and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the theology of it — the wall of the city was dedicated to God, a place he had himself chosen and sanctified by his temple and gracious presence, and so restored to him by prayers, praises, and sacrifices, whence it is often called the holy city.

Adam Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian, remarks that the ancients too consecrated their cities to their gods and held the very walls sacred, citing the ceremonies Ovid records at the founding of Rome by Romulus — a heathen shadow of what Israel here does in truth. The witnesses do not divide. Henry unfolds the meaning, Gill and Keil the occasion, Ellicott the Solomonic pattern, Wesley the holy city given back to God, Clarke the pagan parallel; and together they open the dedication as a sowing of tears reaped in joy, a whole city handed over to the God who alone could keep it.
28:
The preparations begin with the gathering of the singers, and the witnesses trace where they were drawn from. The reformed John Gill takes "the sons of the singers" to mean such of the Levites as were singers, together with their sons trained up to the same office — a hereditary choir summoned for the day. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch identify them more precisely as the members of the three Levitical companies of singers met already at Nehemiah 11:17, and fix the geography of their gathering: they came together out of the Jordan valley round about Jerusalem and from the villages of Netophathi, the fields about Netopha — probably the modern Beit Nettif, some thirteen miles to the south-west — a district known from 1 Chronicles 9:16.

The detail matters, for it shows how far the summons reached. The singers did not all dwell in the city; scattered through the surrounding country, they had to be sought out and brought in, as the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had noted of the whole company — that the Levites were called from all parts of the country to attend, since the city must be dedicated to God and therefore his ministers must be employed in the dedicating of it. When the earlier solemnities were over they had gone home to their posts in the country; now their presence and assistance were again called for.

The witnesses do not divide, and the picture is of a worship that gathered its ministers from a wide field. The praise about to be offered on the wall was not the work of a resident few but of companies drawn in from the villages, the sons following the fathers in the singer's calling, the whole order of Levitical music convened for a single great act of thanksgiving.

There is a quiet fitness in beginning the dedication here. Before a stone of the wall is walked or a sacrifice offered, the historian shows the singers converging on Jerusalem from the plain and the villages — the human material of the coming joy assembling from every quarter. Gill fixes the hereditary choir, Keil the three companies and their country dwellings, Henry the summons that reached to all parts; and together they let the reader watch the thanksgiving take shape from its first movement, as the scattered singers of Israel are gathered to the holy city to lend their voices to the praise its dedication would require.
29:
The gathering of the singers is completed, and the witnesses fix the places from which they came. The reformed John Gill sets "the house of Gilgal" in the champaign country of the plains of Jericho; the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as Beth-Gilgal, the village at the spot where Israel had encamped after crossing the Jordan under Joshua — a name heavy with the memory of the nation's first entrance into the land. From the fields of Geba and of Azmaveth they came also, for, as the verse itself explains, "the singers had builded them villages round about Jerusalem."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the geography, tracing the companies to Beth-gilgal and to the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a telling observation on the settlement: as the Nethinim were settled in Ophel, so the class of Levitical singers were chiefly to be found in villages to the north of the city. The clause about their villages is not incidental; it shows that these ministers of praise had planted their own hamlets in a ring about Jerusalem, near enough to serve the temple, so that when the dedication called them they could be gathered from a manageable compass.

The witnesses do not divide, and the closing clause repays notice. That the singers had built themselves villages round about the city is a small sign of how the return had ordered itself around the house of God — the men whose office was the temple's music settling deliberately within reach of it, so that the daily service and the great occasions alike should never want their voices. The worship of the sanctuary shaped the very map of the countryside.

So the second movement of the preparation is complete: from Gilgal in the Jordan plain, from Geba and Azmaveth, from the villages the singers had made their own, the companies converge on Jerusalem. Gill and Clarke fix Gilgal and its ancient memory, Keil the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, Ellicott the singers' northern villages; and together they show a people whose ministers of praise had settled themselves about the holy city on purpose, ready to be summoned in for the day when the dedicated wall would ring with their thanksgiving. The preparation, patient and geographical, is itself a kind of promise; the very naming of Gilgal and Geba and the singers' villages tells the reader that the joy to come was no sudden thing but a gathering long in the making. The stage is now set, and the next verse will begin the solemnity itself with the purifying of priests and people, gates and wall.
30:
The solemnity opens not with music but with cleansing — "the priests and the Levites purified themselves, and purified the people, and the gates, and the wall" — and the witnesses dwell on the fitness of beginning there. The reformed John Gill takes the purifying to have been done by washing of the body and the clothes, and perhaps by sprinkling the water of purification. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke describes it as consisting in washings and in abstinence from wine and other things otherwise lawful, while the purifying of the gates and walls meant no more than removing all filth from the one and all rubbish from the other.

The grammatical-historical witnesses ground the rite in the law's precedent. Charles Ellicott insists that before consecration to God there must be purification from defilement, and that the text makes it emphatic that both priests and Levites purified themselves — by offerings and ablutions, as at 2 Chronicles 29:15 and Ezra 6:20 — while the gates and the wall were purified by being sprinkled. Keil and Delitzsch judge the cleansing to have been made, on the analogy of 2 Chronicles 29:20, by the offering of sin-offerings and burnt-offerings, according to some special ritual of purification and dedication now unknown to us.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the practical lesson, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry the fullest one. Wesley: those who would be instrumental to sanctify others must first sanctify themselves, and set themselves apart for God with purity of mind and sincerity of intention. Henry presses the same order — we are concerned to cleanse our hands and purify our hearts when any work for God is to pass through them; the priests purified themselves and then the people, then the gates and the wall — and he finds in the sprinkled water a type of the blood of Christ, by which our consciences being purged from dead works we become fit to serve the living God, as Hebrews 9:14 teaches, the water of separation of Numbers 19:9 pointing beyond itself.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke fix the outward washings, Ellicott and Keil the sacrifices and sprinkling that made the rite, Wesley and Henry the inward truth it enshrined. Together they show a dedication that began at the right end — not with the display of joy but with the cleansing that alone could make the joy acceptable, the ministers hallowing themselves before they hallowed the people, and the whole city, walls and gates and all, sprinkled clean before it was given up to God.
31:
The dedication proper begins, and Nehemiah takes the reader into his own act: "Then I brought up the princes of Judah upon the wall, and appointed two great companies of them that gave thanks." The reformed John Gill marks that the wall was broad enough to walk upon, so that a procession of the princes could move along it, the princes of Benjamin being included with those of Judah. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the plan: Nehemiah brought the princes up onto the wall and appointed two great companies of those who gave thanks, forming two solemn processions that went along the wall in opposite directions and halted, facing each other, at the house of God; "the princes of Judah" they take for the princes of the whole community.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the order of the march. Nehemiah divided the priests, Levites, magistrates, and people into two companies, each to go round one half of the wall; both began at the dung gate, the one turning to the right and the other to the left, till they met at the great space opposite the temple, where they offered many sacrifices and rejoiced with exceeding great joy, shouting so that the noise was heard afar off. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the starting-point on the south-west wall, where the chiefs were assembled and then divided into two companies; and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds that half the people went with the princes, the first company turning, as he reads it, toward the south and east.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the scene into its meaning. The princes, priests, and Levites walked round upon the wall in two companies with musical instruments, to signify the dedication of the whole circuit to God; Ezra led the one company and Nehemiah the other, and at length both met in the temple and joined their thanksgivings. The people, he supposes, walked on the ground within and without, that they too might be affected with the mercy for which thanks were given.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the breadth of the wall, Keil and Clarke the two companies and their opposite routes from the dung gate, Ellicott the starting muster, Wesley the direction, Henry the significance; and together they set the great procession in motion. Two companies of thanksgiving, drawn from every rank, mount the very wall so lately raised in fear, and set out in opposite directions to compass the whole city with praise — the stones of the fortification made, for a day, the highway of a national gratitude.
32:
The composition of the first company is now given — "and after them went Hoshaiah, and half of the princes of Judah" — and the witnesses note the mingling of ranks that marched the wall. The reformed John Gill takes it plainly: behind the leading singers went Hoshaiah with the other half of the princes of Judah at their head. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, listing the members of this procession, name after Hoshaiah a file of princes — Azariah, Ezra, Meshullam, Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, and Jeremiah — followed by certain of the priests' sons with trumpets, so that the company was a deliberate blend of the civil and the sacred.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott seizes on precisely that blend. These verses, he observes, show that the clerical and the lay elements were mingled in the procession — princes and priests walking together, the rulers of the people and the ministers of the temple joined in one company of thanksgiving. The dedication was not the affair of the clergy alone, nor of the magistrates alone, but of the whole restored commonwealth moving as one.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had already fixed the order of the two companies, with Ezra leading the van of this first procession and Nehemiah bringing up the rear of the other; and half the princes went with each, so that the leadership of the nation was itself divided between the two thanksgiving bands and displayed upon the wall. The men who governed Judah walked its ramparts in praise, and their walking was itself a kind of confession that the city they ruled belonged to God.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse, brief as it is, carries the chapter's larger note. What is being dedicated is a city, and a city is its people; so the historian is careful to record not only the singers and the sacrifices but the princes who marched with them, the great men of Judah taking their appointed place in the solemnity. Gill fixes Hoshaiah at the head of his half, Keil the file of names behind him, Ellicott the mingling of lay and priestly, Henry the ordered leadership; and together they let the reader see the whole society of the return — rulers and priests, singers and people — gathered into a single act of thanks, the government of the city and the worship of the temple moving side by side along the dedicated wall.
33:
The procession's roll continues — "and Azariah, Ezra, and Meshullam" — and the witnesses are careful to keep one Ezra distinct from another. The reformed John Gill warns at once that this is not Ezra the priest and scribe, who has his own honoured place in the march at v.36, but one of the princes bearing the same name; the great scribe is not to be confused with a namesake among the lay chiefs. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, weighing the names, suggests that this Ezra is probably the same person as the Azariah that precedes him — the two forms standing for one man, as often in these lists where a name shifts its shape.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the names within the file of princes who followed Hoshaiah in the first company — Azariah, Ezra, Meshullam, and the rest — the lay leaders of Judah walking the wall in thanksgiving before the priestly musicians who came after them. The list is not a random jumble but the ordered company of the nation's chief men.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the whole scene in view: this was the first of the two companies, with Ezra the scribe leading its van and the princes following, all moving toward the house of God where the two processions would meet. The naming of the princes, obscure as most of them now are, serves the historian's purpose of showing that the great men of Judah were personally present and personally engaged, lending their own feet and voices to the dedication.

The witnesses do not divide, though Gill guards the identity of the scribe and Ellicott ventures the equation of Azariah and Ezra. What they share is the sense that even these bare names matter, for they record who took part. That a prince named Ezra should march in the same company as, though distinct from, Ezra the scribe is a small caution against hasty reading; and that the historian should trouble to name him at all is a token of the honour attaching to a share in so joyful a solemnity. Gill separates the two Ezras, Ellicott joins Azariah to one of them, Keil files them among the princes, Henry sets them in the moving company; and together they let the reader follow the first procession along the wall, prince by prince, toward the temple where its thanksgiving would be joined to the other's.
34:
The file of the first company runs on — "Judah, and Benjamin, and Shemaiah, and Jeremiah" — and the witnesses first settle what these words are. The reformed John Gill, following the Jewish commentator Jarchi, insists that Judah and Benjamin here are not the tribes but the personal names of two of the princes; the reader who takes them for the tribal divisions mistakes the sense, for the verse is still numbering the individual men who walked in the procession. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls it a singular collocation — the laity of Judah and Benjamin set here between priests before and priests after — and reads it as one more mark of that mingling of the sacred and the civil which the whole procession displayed.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch place the names within the ordered company that followed Hoshaiah — the princes Azariah, Ezra, Meshullam, Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, and Jeremiah — the lay chiefs of the nation marching in their appointed rank before the priests' sons with their trumpets. The arrangement is deliberate: laymen and ministers interwoven, so that no order of the people should be missing from the thanksgiving.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the larger picture, for this is still the first of the two companies, Ezra leading its van and the princes following toward the house of God. The presence of these named men, lay and priestly together, embodied what the dedication meant — the whole society of the return, and not its clergy only, giving thanks for the city God had let them build.

The witnesses do not divide, though the reading turns on Gill's careful point that Judah and Benjamin are men, not tribes. Ellicott's observation about the collocation only sharpens the same truth: the historian has set lay princes in the midst of priests on purpose, that the reader may see the two elements of the nation moving as one. Gill fixes the names as persons, Ellicott the mingling they exemplify, Keil their place in the file, Henry the meaning of the whole; and together they let even this string of names testify that the dedication of the wall gathered every rank into a single company, the laymen of Judah and Benjamin walking the ramparts of the holy city shoulder to shoulder with the ministers of its temple, all bound for the same meeting-place of praise. That the historian should preserve even these all-but-forgotten names is his way of honouring the men who came, and of teaching that in the sight of God no share in the dedication of his city, however humble the sharer, went unrecorded.
35:
The first company is completed by its musicians — "and certain of the priests' sons with trumpets" — and the witnesses fix both the instrument and the man who led them. The reformed John Gill notes that these were the priests' sons appointed to blow the trumpets on this occasion, for the sounding of the trumpets belonged to the priests. The instrument was not a matter of taste but of law: the silver trumpet was the priestly instrument, and so it was the sons of Aaron, not the Levitical singers, who carried it in the procession.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the leader named here — Zechariah the son of Jonathan — back through his line to Asaph, and set him at the head of the section of Levitical musicians that followed this company, his brethren enumerated in the verse that follows. They played, the text says, with the musical instruments of David the man of God, an ordinance Keil grounds in 1 Chronicles 23:5 and 2 Chronicles 29:26; and they judge, from the seven priests named again at v.41, that seven trumpeters marched with each company.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the point that nothing in the music was improvised: no part of the service deviated from sacred precedent, the instruments being those of David, so that the thanksgiving on the wall was offered in the very forms the founder of the temple's worship had appointed. The descent of Zechariah from Asaph, the trumpets in priestly hands, the Davidic instruments — all bind the day's joy to the ancient pattern.

The witnesses do not divide, and the arrangement they describe is significant. The two great sounds of Israel's worship were joined in this company: the priests' trumpets and the Levites' stringed instruments, the one by the sons of Aaron and the other by the sons of Asaph, each keeping to its appointed office. Gill fixes the trumpets to the priests, Keil the Asaphite leader and the Davidic instruments, Ellicott the fidelity to precedent; and together they show a thanksgiving that was jubilant but never disorderly — a music old as David, offered by the men the law had set apart for it, so that when the wall rang with trumpet and psaltery it rang in the forms the God of Israel had himself prescribed. There is order even in the joy: the priest to his trumpet, the Levite to his harp, the son of Asaph to his appointed place, so that the exuberance of the day was carried on the rails of an ancient and settled discipline.
36:
The musicians of the first company are named — "and his brethren, Shemaiah, and Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, and Judah, Hanani" — and two things draw the witnesses: the instruments they played and the great man who went before them. The reformed John Gill takes "his brethren" for the brethren of Zechariah, the priest's son of the previous verse, the file of players who followed him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add that they went "with the musical instruments of David the man of God," and then trace the route of the procession: from the wall by the dung gate it passed to the fountain gate and, going straight before them, up by the stairs of the city of David — the stairs that Nehemiah 3:15 sets on the eastern slope of Zion — over the house of David, to the water gate eastward, though they own that the topographical statements are not now quite intelligible.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fastens on the last clause of the verse — "and Ezra the scribe before them" — and gives it its due weight. No part of the service, he repeats, deviated from sacred precedent, the instruments being David's; and the place of Ezra is significant, for between the singers and the princes walked the man who was the greatest in dignity though but the second in office. The reformer of the people's religion led the procession of praise.

There is a quiet honour in that arrangement. Nehemiah, the governor, would bring up the rear of the other company; Ezra, the priest and scribe, leads the van of this one. The two men who had together restored the law and the city are set at the head and the tail of the two great thanksgiving processions, each in his place, the whole solemnity framed between them.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the brethren of Zechariah, Keil the Davidic instruments and the ascending route by the stairs of the city of David, Ellicott the dignity of Ezra walking before them. Together they show the first company moving up from the low ground by the fountain gate to the height of the water gate, singers and players and princes in order, with Ezra the scribe at their head — a march that was at once a circuit of the wall and a solemn ascent toward the house of God, made in the forms of David and led by the man who had brought Israel back to the book of the law.
37:
The route of the first company is traced further — "and at the fountain gate, which was over against them, they went up by the stairs of the city of David, at the going up of the wall, above the house of David, even unto the water gate eastward" — and the witnesses follow it as best the ancient topography allows. The reformed John Gill fixes the fountain gate over against them, to the south of the dung gate where the procession had begun, so that the company, having set out at the one, now reached the other and turned upward.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the ascent: from the fountain gate the procession went straight before it, up by the stairs of the city of David — the stairs that Nehemiah 3:15 places on the eastern slope of Zion — at the going up of the wall, above the house of David, to the water gate eastward. They confess, candidly, that the statements are not now quite intelligible to us, the exact line of the march being lost with the ancient city; but the general course is plain enough — from the low southern gate up the steep eastern side toward the temple.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, comparing the circuit with the account of the building in Nehemiah 3, keeps the reader mindful that this first company had the shorter route, mounting the eastern wall toward the house of God, while the second would take the longer northern round. Nothing in the march, he had insisted, departed from the sacred precedents the day was honouring.

The witnesses do not divide, and their patience with an obscure topography is itself instructive. Rather than force the ruined map into a false clarity, they trace what can be traced and own what cannot — the gates, the stairs, the ascent by the city of David, the water gate at the end — and leave the rest to honest uncertainty. Gill fixes the fountain gate south of the dung gate, Keil the ascent by the stairs of the city of David, Ellicott the shorter eastern route; and together they let the reader walk with the first company up the steep eastern rampart of Jerusalem, from the low gate by the pool to the height above the house of David, drawing ever nearer the temple where the two thanksgivings would meet — the very stones of the wall, so lately built, made the path of a solemn and ascending praise.
38:
The narrative turns to the second procession — "and the other company of them that gave thanks went over against them, and I after them" — and the witnesses follow its longer, opposite course. The reformed John Gill sets it on the left hand, taking the northern part of the wall, while the first had gone to the right. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the whole of its march: the second company went in the contrary direction, Nehemiah himself following after them with half the people upon the wall, from beyond the tower of the furnaces even unto the broad wall, and on past the gates named in the verse that follows.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, comparing the route with the record of the building in Nehemiah 3, gives the clearest map of it: this company had the longer way, proceeding to the left, rounding the northern "broad wall," passing the sheep gate, and so coming at last to meet the priestly company near the prison gate, with the temple straight before them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke pauses over the "broad wall," which he supposes to have been a place designed for a public promenade, or a parade for the assembling of the temple's guard.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the meaning of Nehemiah's own place in the march. The other half of the princes and priests, who likewise gave thanks, went to the left, and Nehemiah brought up the rear — as Ezra had led the van of the first company. The two men who had restored the city and the law thus took the head and the foot of the two processions, the whole solemnity moving between them.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill sets the company on the northern wall, Keil traces its route from the tower of the furnaces to the broad wall, Ellicott its long circuit by the sheep gate to the prison gate, Clarke the promenade of the broad wall, Henry the governor bringing up the rear. Together they show the second great band of thanksgiving setting out in the opposite direction from the first, so that between them the two companies would compass the entire circuit of the wall and enclose the whole city in a ring of praise — Nehemiah walking last of all, behind the princes and the people, upon the very rampart his labour had raised. There is a fitness in the governor walking last, behind the people he served, upon the wall he had built; the leader who had gone before them in the toil now followed after them in the thanksgiving.
39:
The northern route of the second company is traced past its landmarks — "from above the gate of Ephraim, and above the old gate, and above the fish gate, and the tower of Hananeel, and the tower of Meah, even unto the sheep gate: and they stood still in the prison gate." The reformed John Gill notes the first of these, the gate of Ephraim, so named because it led toward the territory where that tribe had formerly dwelt. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a telling detail about it: the gate of Ephraim is not mentioned in the account of the repairing of the wall in Nehemiah 3, having apparently remained comparatively intact, together with the neighbouring stretch of the broad wall — a portion the enemy's destruction had spared.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the reader along the whole file of gates and towers, from the gate of Ephraim by the old gate and the fish gate, past the tower of Hananeel and the tower of Meah, to the sheep gate, where the company drew near the prison gate and halted. The route is the reverse of the first company's, sweeping round the north of the city toward the temple.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fixes the meaning of that halt. They "stood still" at the prison gate, he explains, waiting — as their brethren of the other company also waited — that the two might go together in due order into the house of God, there to perfect the solemnity. The procession did not straggle into the temple piecemeal; it paused, that both companies might enter as one.

The witnesses do not divide, and that pause is the point on which they leave the verse. Two great bands had set out in opposite directions to compass the whole wall; now, their circuits nearly done, they stand still within sight of each other and of the sanctuary, holding their place till the moment of joined entrance. Gill fixes the gate of Ephraim, Ellicott its survival from the ruin, Keil the file of gates and towers, Wesley the reason of the halt; and together they show the second company brought at last to the prison gate, its long northern march complete, waiting in ordered stillness for the other company to arrive, that the two thanksgivings might be offered not separately but together in the house of their God. The stillness at the prison gate is itself eloquent, a pause of discipline in the midst of joy, that the praise might rise not in disorder but in the ordered unity the whole day had aimed at.
40:
The two circuits are done, and the companies meet: "so stood the two companies of them that gave thanks in the house of God, and I, and the half of the rulers with me." The reformed John Gill marks the convergence — having made their procession upon the wall by different ways, the two companies met in the temple, that is, in its great court, for no lesser space could hold them. The whole ring of praise that had begun at the dung gate now closes at the sanctuary.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott refines the picture. They stood first outside, he says, and only afterward entered to present their offerings; but the main interest of the day was the professional worship under the open heavens — the thanksgiving of the companies in the temple court, beneath the sky, before ever the sacrifices were brought within. The other grammatical-historical witness, Keil and Delitzsch, simply records the two companies standing together in the house of God, the goal toward which both processions had moved.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the meeting its weight. At length both companies met in the temple, he says, where they joined their thanksgivings — the two streams of praise that had gone out in opposite directions now flowing together into one. Nehemiah stood there with the half of the rulers who had followed him, even as Ezra stood with the other half; the leaders of the nation, divided for the march, were reunited at the altar.

The witnesses do not divide, and the scene they describe is the very heart of the solemnity. The dedication had encircled the city with two moving companies; now those companies stand still and together in the house of God, and what was a procession becomes a congregation. The wall had been the highway of praise; the temple is its destination. Gill fixes the meeting in the great court, Ellicott the worship under the open heaven, Keil the two companies standing as one, Henry the joined thanksgivings; and together they show the whole circuit of the city gathered at last into a single act of worship, the two bands that had compassed the ramparts now merged before the sanctuary, ready to offer the sacrifices and lift the songs in which the dedication would reach its height. And there is something moving in the reunion: the leaders parted for the march are joined again at the altar, the two halves of the nation's chief men standing together where the two circuits close, so that the meeting of the companies is also the mending of what the procession had briefly divided.
41:
The priests of the second company are numbered — "and the priests; Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets" — and the witnesses mark the symmetry with the first. The reformed John Gill notes only that the priests stood there also, in the house of God, whose names the verse now gives. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that these names, like those of the priests and Levites at v.35, are personal, not to be found in the earlier lists of the register — the men who actually served on this day, rather than the houses to which they belonged.

The number is not accidental. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch had reckoned, from the seven priests named here, that seven trumpeters marched with each company; and so the second band, like the first, had its full complement of the sons of Aaron sounding the silver trumpets. The two processions were built to match: each with its princes, its singers, its priestly trumpeters, so that when they met in the temple the one answered the other in every part.

The trumpet, as at v.35, was the priestly instrument, and its sounding by seven priests in each company gave the thanksgiving its full and legal voice. The dedication was no informal rejoicing but a service ordered down to the number of its trumpeters, offered in the forms the law prescribed and the founders of the temple's worship had appointed.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill sets the priests in their place, Ellicott marks their names as those of the living servants of the day, Keil counts them at seven to match the first company. Together they show the second procession complete and answering to the first — seven priests with trumpets here as there — so that the two companies standing in the house of God formed one balanced whole, the trumpets of the sons of Aaron ready to sound from both sides of the joined congregation. What began as two files upon the wall is now two matched choirs before the altar, and the naming of these seven priests, obscure as they are, is the historian's quiet way of showing that nothing needful to the solemnity was wanting, and that the praise about to break forth would be sounded in due and appointed order. The symmetry is deliberate and instructive: God's worship is not the poorer for being ordered, and the very matching of the two companies, priest for priest and trumpet for trumpet, was itself part of the honour done to him.
42:
The trumpeters of the second company are completed, and the singers lift their voice: "and Maaseiah, and Shemaiah, and Eleazar, and Uzzi, and Jehohanan, and Malchijah, and Elam, and Ezer. And the singers sang loud, with Jezrahiah their overseer." The reformed John Gill takes the eight names to be, like those before them, priests who blew the trumpets, so that the full priestly complement of the second company is now told. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix on the closing clause: the singers "sang loud" — made their voice to be heard — under Jezrahiah their overseer, who led the united choirs in the great outburst of praise.

Here the whole solemnity gathers to its sound. The two companies stand together in the house of God; the priests of both, seven and seven, hold their trumpets; and now the singers, no longer processing but stationed before the sanctuary, lift the psalm at full strength under their appointed leader. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott had insisted throughout that nothing in the music departed from the sacred precedents of David; and this loud, ordered singing, led by a named overseer, is the fruit of that fidelity — a jubilant noise, but a disciplined one.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse marks the moment the dedication becomes fully vocal.
