All that the register had quietly prepared — the singers gathered from their villages, the trumpets set in priestly hands, the answering companies ordered ward against ward — now issues in a single swell of sound, the choirs of Jerusalem singing aloud with all their might. Jezrahiah stands over them as Mattaniah had once stood "over the thanksgiving" at v.8, the office of leading the praise handed on and now exercised at the very climax of the day.

Gill numbers the priests with their trumpets, Keil fixes the loud singing and its overseer, Ellicott the fidelity to David's forms. Together they show the two companies, met at last in the temple, breaking into a thanksgiving loud enough to be heard, the trumpets of the priests and the voices of the singers joined under Jezrahiah in one great acknowledgment of the God who had let them build the wall. The next verse will add the sacrifices and the joy of the whole people; here the sound itself is described, the choirs of the holy city singing aloud for the mercy that had encircled them, and their song lifted, in due order and full voice, before the house of God.
43:
The dedication reaches its climax in sacrifice and overflowing joy — "also that day they offered great sacrifices, and rejoiced: for God had made them rejoice with great joy" — and the witnesses dwell on the gladness and its source. The reformed John Gill reads the "great sacrifices" as many, and of the larger cattle, oxen; being in good part peace offerings, the people feasted upon them, so that the day was kept as a festival. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the order of the verse: it is full of joy, but before the rejoicing comes the abundant offering of sacrifices — the feasting founded upon the altar, the gladness resting on atonement.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry enters most fully into the scene. The people greatly rejoiced; the princes, priests, and Levites testified their joy by great sacrifices, the sound of trumpet, and songs of praise, while the common people testified theirs by loud shouts heard afar off — further, he notes, than the more harmonious sound of the music. And these honest shouts God graciously accepts, for he overlooks not the zealous services of mean people, though there is in them little of art. Henry fastens on the cause the text assigns: God "had made them rejoice with great joy," giving them both matter for joy and hearts to rejoice; his providence had made them safe, and then his grace made them cheerful and thankful, the baffled malice of their enemies adding to the gladness.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley notes with tenderness that the wives also and the children rejoiced, and their hosannas were not despised but are recorded to their praise; for all that share in public mercies ought to join in public thanksgivings. The joy of a rescued people was not the clergy's alone, nor the men's alone, but ran through the whole household of Israel.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gathers the chapter's long preparation into a single burst of gratitude. The joy of Jerusalem, the text says, was heard even afar off — the noise of a city that had sown in tears now reaping in triumph. Gill fixes the peace offerings and the festival, Ellicott the sacrifice that grounds the joy, Henry the God who authored it and the shouts of the common people, Wesley the wives and children caught up in it. Together they show the dedication reaching its height not in ceremony merely but in an unfeigned and universal gladness, a whole people rejoicing before God because God himself had made them rejoice — the walls of the holy city ringing, for a day, with a thanksgiving loud enough to carry beyond its gates.
44:
The joy of the dedication bears lasting fruit in the ordering of the temple's support — "at that time were some appointed over the chambers for the treasures, for the offerings, for the firstfruits, and for the tithes" — and the witnesses read it as the practical outcome of a thankful heart. The reformed John Gill notes that on the very day of the dedication, while the people were in so good a disposition, certain of the priests were appointed overseers of the chambers set apart for treasuries, to lay up safely the offerings and see them put to their proper use. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark it as part of the joint work of Nehemiah and Ezra in restoring the enactments of the law: men were set over the chambers to gather into them, out of the fields of the cities, the portions the law appointed for the priests and Levites, "for Judah rejoiced for the priests and for the Levites that waited."

That last clause is the hinge, and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses it: the temple service being now restored to something like its completeness in David's day, the people everywhere took pleasure in its ministrations and provided amply for them, whence the very need of officers to take charge of the treasuries of firstfruits and tithes. The joy issued in generosity, and the generosity required order.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the whole lesson. When the solemnities of a thanksgiving leave such impressions that both ministers and people are more careful of their duty afterward, then they are indeed acceptable to God; and so it was here. The people rejoiced for the priests and Levites that waited, having comfort in their ministers and gladness in their diligence; and because many were careless and would not bring their dues unless called upon, some were appointed to gather them in, that the ministers' portion might not be lost for want of demanding — a service, Henry says, to both the ministers and the people. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley strikes the same note: the people rejoiced for the eminent gifts of their ministers, for the benefit of their ministry, and for the provision now made, that so they might wholly wait upon their office; and the surest way for ministers to gain their people's affection is to wait on their ministry.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the overseers of the treasuries, Keil the gathering of the law's portions, Ellicott the ample provision born of the people's pleasure, Henry the careful duty a thanksgiving should leave behind, Wesley the ministers who wait on their office. Together they show a joy that did not evaporate with the day but settled into the steady maintenance of God's house — the gladness of the dedication translated at once into treasuries, officers, and portions, so that the worship so joyfully restored might be soberly and permanently sustained.
45:
The renewed order of the temple is described in the faithfulness of its ministers — "and both the singers and the porters kept the ward of their God, and the ward of the purification, according to the commandment of David, and of Solomon his son." The reformed John Gill sets out their double diligence: the singers kept their turns in course, not wanting to officiate on any occasion beyond the daily services, and the porters diligently kept the gates of the temple, that no person or thing ceremonially unclean should enter. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read "kept the ward of their God" to mean that they faithfully and punctually performed all that pertained to their office, both toward God and toward the purification, "according to the commandment of David and of Solomon his son," an ordinance they trace to 2 Chronicles 8:14 and 1 Chronicles 24.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would parse the verse a little differently, taking the priests and Levites to keep the ward of their God and of purification, and the singers and porters likewise; and he glosses "to keep the ward" as to observe the regular times and seasons of sacrifice and thanksgiving. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads "the ward" as the charge God had prescribed, and in particular the charge of purification — the care that no unclean person or thing should enter into the house or courts of the Lord.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into the fruit of the dedication's joy. The ministers were now more careful than before of their work; the respect the people had shown them encouraged them to diligence, so that the singers kept the ward of their God, attending in due time to their office, and the porters kept the ward of purification, preserving the purity of the temple by denying admission to the ceremonially unclean. When the joy of the Lord thus engages us to our duty and enlarges us in it, Henry adds, it is an earnest of that everlasting bliss which the perfection of holiness will bring.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the singers' courses and the porters' guard, Keil their punctual office under David and Solomon, Ellicott the regular seasons they observed, Wesley the charge of purification, Henry the diligence the thanksgiving had quickened. Together they show a worship not only joyfully restored but faithfully kept — the ministers holding their several wards according to the ancient command, the gates guarded against defilement, the temple's purity maintained; the gladness of the dedication settling, as true joy will, into the steady and watchful performance of duty in the house of God.
46:
The faithfulness of the singers is grounded in an ancient institution — "for in the days of David and Asaph of old there were chief of the singers, and songs of praise and thanksgiving unto God" — and the witnesses honour the antiquity of the order. The reformed John Gill explains that in the days of David and Asaph there were chief of the singers set over the rest, to instruct them and see that they did their work aright — Asaph, with Heman and Jeduthun and their sons, heading the temple's music from the first. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as tracing the current arrangement back to its source: the singers of Nehemiah's day did but continue what David and Asaph had established of old, the songs of praise and thanksgiving unto God being no new invention but the revival of an ancient service.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the spirit of the appeal in two words: "of old." Always, he observes, there is a reverence shown for the old precedents — the historian grounding the present practice not on his own authority but on the venerable pattern of David, so that the restored worship draws its warrant from antiquity. What was done in the dedication and kept afterward was done because David had appointed it long before.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse serves to bind the whole chapter's music to its origin. The choirs gathered from the villages, the answering companies on the wall, the loud singing under Jezrahiah, the daily ward of the singers now maintained — all rest upon the institution of David and Asaph, revived after the captivity and carried on unbroken. The return did not improvise its praise; it recovered it.

There is a quiet doctrine in the historian's backward glance. The reformers of the second temple, Nehemiah and Ezra, were not innovators but restorers, and their care was to bring back the old ways of the house of God rather than to devise new ones. Gill fixes the chief singers of David's day, Keil the continuity of the service, Ellicott the reverence for old precedent. Together they show a worship whose authority lay behind it — the songs of praise and thanksgiving reaching back to David and Asaph "of old," and the men who kept the ward in Nehemiah's day standing in a succession of singers as ancient as the monarchy itself, so that the joy of the dedicated city was the joy of an old and hallowed order made new.
47:
The chapter closes with the whole nation providing for its ministers — "and all Israel in the days of Zerubbabel, and in the days of Nehemiah, gave the portions of the singers and the porters, every day his portion" — and the witnesses read it as the seal upon the restored worship. The reformed John Gill notes that while these two men governed, the people did their duty and punctually paid the Levites their dues at the proper season. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains the arrangement: the singers and porters were supported by the people at large, each receiving his portion daily; the things provided for sacred uses were delivered by the people to the Levites, and the Levites in turn presented them to the priests, the children of Aaron — this presenting being what the text calls "sanctifying" them, the dedicating of them to the holy uses for which they were designed.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the order of that chain: between the people and the priests came the Levites, who received the tithe and gave the priests their "tithe of the tithe," according to the command of Numbers 18:26. The whole nation's offering passed upward through the appointed hands, each order taking its share and passing on the rest.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the conscience in it: they set apart the firstfruits and tithes from their own share and devoted them to the Levites, and the Levites did the like by the tithe of the tithes; thus all conscientiously paid their dues and did not profane what God had sanctified by turning it to common use. When what is contributed for the support of religion is given with an eye to God, Wesley adds, it is sanctified, and will cause the blessing to rest upon the house and all that is in it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had struck the same note, that the tithes, here called holy things, being contributed with an eye to God and his honour, are sanctified and accepted of him, and bring the blessing to rest, as Ezekiel 44:30 promises. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the punctual payment, Clarke the chain of provision and the sense of "sanctify," Ellicott the tithe of the tithe, Wesley the conscience that would not profane holy things, Henry the blessing that follows a consecrated gift. Together they close the chapter where it belongs — not in the passing joy of a festival but in the settled, daily faithfulness of a people who maintained the ministers of God's house, all Israel giving every day its portion, and the whole offering, from the people's hand through the Levites to the sons of Aaron, sanctified to the God whose worship it sustained.
